tail.sun: Our nearest star — a 1.4-million-km plasma furnace, fusing 600 million tons of hydrogen every second.
tail.moon: Drifting 3.8 cm farther from Earth every year — slowly stretching the length of our day.
tail.jupiter: So massive it could swallow every other planet in the solar system combined — and its Great Red Spot has been raging for at least 350 years.
tail.saturn: Less dense than water — if you could find an ocean big enough, Saturn would float.
tail.mars: Home to Olympus Mons, a volcano nearly three times the height of Mount Everest.
tail.venus: The hottest world in the solar system — its CO₂ atmosphere traps heat at 465 °C, day and night.
tail.mercury: The smallest planet — its surface swings from 430 °C in sunlight to −180 °C at night.
tail.uranus: Tipped on its side — it rolls around the Sun instead of spinning upright.
tail.neptune: The windiest planet — supersonic storms tear across it at over 2,000 km/h.

recognize.jupiter: Steady, golden-white. Doesn't twinkle the way stars do.

recognize.venus: Brighter than every star. Often called the evening or morning star.
recognize.mercury: A bright point near the horizon, low in twilight.
recognize.uranus: Pale blue-green dot — needs binoculars and a star chart.
recognize.neptune: Pale blue dot — needs a telescope and patience.

events.subtitle: Mark your calendar. Tap any card to see how to observe.

lunar_eclipse_mar3.body: The full Moon drifts through Earth's umbra and glows deep copper-red. Totality lasts 58 minutes; the full event runs about 3.5 hours from first to last contact.
lunar_eclipse_mar3.peak: Mid-totality 11:33 UTC (visible from Asia, Australia, the Pacific)
lunar_eclipse_mar3.moon: Full Moon — and the eclipse star itself
lunar_eclipse_mar3.gear: Naked eye; binoculars sharpen the colour
lunar_eclipse_mar3.tip: No filters needed. Find a clear horizon and start watching as the Moon enters the penumbra — the dimming begins subtly, then accelerates into umbral contact.

lyrids.body: A steady spring shower with a Zenithal Hourly Rate near 18, and occasional outbursts that triple it. Streaks are bright, fast, and often leave persistent trains.
lyrids.moon: Waxing crescent — sets mid-evening, dark for the post-midnight peak
lyrids.gear: Naked eye; reclining chair beats craning your neck
lyrids.tip: Look up once the radiant in Lyra is high (after midnight). Let your eyes adapt for 20 minutes — no phone screens, no flashlights.

mars_saturn_conj.body: Mars and Saturn pass about 1.3° apart — close enough to share one binocular field. Mars glows steady red; Saturn shows pale gold with rings barely tilted. Both sit very low in bright dawn twilight, so this one rewards effort.
mars_saturn_conj.peak: Pre-dawn April 20, in the last hour before sunrise, very low in the east
mars_saturn_conj.moon: Waxing crescent — sets in the evening, no interference at dawn
mars_saturn_conj.gear: 10×50 binoculars frame both; a small scope shows Saturn's rings
mars_saturn_conj.tip: Be set up an hour before sunrise. Mars is the redder, steady dot; Saturn the steadier gold. Both ride low — an unobstructed eastern horizon makes or breaks the view.

perseids.body: The summer classic — peak Zenithal Hourly Rate of 100, with bright fireballs that often leave smoke trains lasting several seconds.
perseids.moon: New Moon — the darkest possible sky
perseids.gear: Naked eye only; cameras with 24mm+ wide lenses catch the bright ones
perseids.tip: Drive 30+ minutes out of city light. Lie back, face northeast where Perseus rises, and just watch. Counting meteors keeps you alert.

solar_eclipse_aug12.body: The path of totality crosses Greenland, Iceland, and northern Spain — about 2 minutes 18 seconds of full darkness. Across the rest of Europe and North Africa it's a deep partial.
solar_eclipse_aug12.peak: Greatest eclipse 17:46 UTC — early evening across Europe
solar_eclipse_aug12.gear: ISO-12312-2 solar filters or eclipse glasses, always
solar_eclipse_aug12.tip: Never look directly without certified protection. If you lack filters, build a pinhole projector — a single hole in card stock projects a crescent Sun onto any flat surface.

saturn_opp.body: Saturn rises as the Sun sets and shines all night, at its brightest (mag +0.4) and biggest of the year. Rings are tilted a few degrees — slowly reopening after the 2025 edge-on event.
saturn_opp.peak: Rises at sunset; transits highest around local midnight
saturn_opp.moon: Last quarter — rises near midnight; early-evening hours stay dark
saturn_opp.gear: Telescope at 80×+ to split the rings; even a 60mm achromat shows them clearly
saturn_opp.tip: Wait until Saturn climbs above 30° altitude — atmospheric turbulence smears the view at low angles. Use medium magnification first; push higher only when the seeing is steady.

geminids.body: The most reliable shower of the year — slow, colour-tinted meteors at a Zenithal Hourly Rate near 120. Often produces bright multicoloured fireballs.
geminids.peak: 02:00 local time, December 14, with the radiant nearly overhead
geminids.moon: Waxing crescent (~25%) — sets by mid-evening, leaving prime hours dark
geminids.gear: Naked eye; serious thermal layers (this is winter)
geminids.tip: Once the crescent Moon sets in mid-evening, face anywhere — the radiant in Gemini climbs overhead, so meteors fall in every direction.

howItWorks.title: How a capture is proved
howItWorks.intro: What happens between a mount slewing and a record on chain — and, more usefully, what the system refuses to do. Each step below names the code that enforces it.
howItWorks.step1Title: The mount says where it pointed
howItWorks.step1Body: A phone photograph of the sky proves very little about where the camera was aimed — which is why verifying one takes a vision model, EXIF, a dedup hash, a reverse-image lookup and a visibility cross-check, and still returns a confidence rather than a fact. A node capture starts from the other end. The mount reports the coordinates it slewed to from its own encoders, and the agent records them beside the frame. The pointing is not a claim anyone made about the picture; it is what the instrument did.
howItWorks.step2Title: The frame is signed where it was taken
howItWorks.step2Body: The agent signs the capture at the node, before it leaves the owner’s network. Stellar never receives node credentials and never addresses a mount or a camera: every command travels through the adapter, expires, is idempotent by command id, and is re-validated locally by the node against its own altitude envelope, horizon mask and Sun avoidance. A command the cloud approved and the node considers unsafe does not move the telescope.
howItWorks.step3Title: Provenance is declared by the adapter, never by the client
howItWorks.step3Body: The capture endpoint asks adapterFor(node) what a frame taken this second is worth, and ignores the request body entirely — there is no field a client could set. It is asked at the moment of capture rather than read off the adapter once, because a node platform can be connected and still running its own simulator, and being wired to a telescope is not the same as that telescope being the thing that took the picture. Every uncertainty resolves downward: an unreachable node, a late heartbeat, a reply we do not recognise, all mean simulated.
howItWorks.step4Title: One gate decides what a frame is worth
howItWorks.step4Body: admitToCollection() admits a capture only when its provenance is exactly "instrument", and returns the reason when it refuses. Minting, awarding Stars and writing an observation all pass through that one function rather than each surface remembering to check. A rule enforced in six places is a rule that will eventually be enforced in five.
howItWorks.step5Title: An admitted capture becomes an ordinary observation
howItWorks.step5Body: Nothing about the record is special-cased. An admitted capture is written to the same observation log a phone photograph writes to, with the same verification columns and the same chain references — so the gallery, the feed, the passport and the share images keep working with no change at all. A stronger input, in the same shape.
howItWorks.step6Title: The oracle records it on chain
howItWorks.step6Body: The Proof-of-Observation program stores each observation as its own account, seeded by the hash of the frame — which means re-recording the same image fails at account creation, and dedup is a property of the chain rather than a query we remember to run. Attestations are oracle-signed and written gaslessly on the user’s behalf. The user signed up with an email and never touches a key.
howItWorks.refusalsTitle: What a simulated frame cannot do
howItWorks.refusalsIntro: The simulator is open to everyone and needs no account. It models the real optical train, the real slew times and the real safety envelope, and it refuses the same targets the instrument would, for the same reasons. What it produces is a teaching tool, not evidence.
howItWorks.refusalLog: Be written to the observation log
howItWorks.refusalSell: Be sold, printed, or delivered as a photograph
howItWorks.refusalsNote: Simulated captures are stored and shown, always labelled. They are never quietly mixed in with instrument frames.
howItWorks.whyTitle: Why the rail exists before the telescope does
howItWorks.whyP1: In July 2026 a certify-all window put fourteen compressed NFTs on Solana mainnet carrying <m>Verified: yes</m> for observations that nothing had verified. They are still there; they cannot be unwritten, and the honest count of genuinely verified mints from that period is zero.
howItWorks.whyP2: A simulator that could mint would be that same mistake, made deliberately and at scale. So the gate was built before the first instrument was wired, while it was still cheap to be strict — and the network was designed so that the only way to produce a record is to actually point a telescope at the sky.
howItWorks.tonightCount: <n>{live}</n> of <n>{total}</n> {total, plural, one {instrument is} other {instruments are}} wired to real hardware.
howItWorks.tonightWaiting: Until that number moves, every frame the network produces is simulated and is marked as such everywhere it appears — including here. The steps above are built and enforced; what they are waiting for is first light.
howItWorks.tonightMixed: The rest run on the simulator and are labelled wherever they appear.

operator.title: Put your telescope to work
operator.lead: Most instruments are used a handful of nights a year. On the clear nights you are not out with yours, someone else can be — and you are paid for it.
operator.keepLead: Your share rises with hours actually delivered — not nights listed, not a subscription. An instrument that has run 150 hours of other people’s sessions has been aligned, cleaned and unparked 150 hours’ worth, and that is the only number worth paying for.
operator.keepNote: At three sessions a night on a hundred clear nights, a season pays for the effort. A session that clouds out refunds the customer in full and costs you nothing.
operator.needs1: A computerised GoTo mount, and somewhere it can stay set up.
operator.needs2: A camera and a mini-PC to run the agent on.
operator.needs3: A network connection, and a horizon you would observe from yourself.
operator.needsNote: There is no box to buy. If you already run ASCOM, Alpaca or INDI, the software installs on what you have.
operator.dryRunNote: Nothing has settled yet. {name} runs on the simulator until the instrument is wired, and simulated sessions pay nothing and count for nothing — the figures above start moving the night it goes live.
operator.formLead: No commitment, and nothing to install yet. Listing opens as the first partner nodes come online, oldest registrations first.

operator.doneLead: We will write when the first partner nodes are commissioned, and we will tell you plainly what your rig needs.

simulator.how1: Public-domain NASA and ESA imagery supplies the content. Everything else is computed: the target is scaled to its true angular size at the current focal length, smeared by the seeing, shifted frame to frame by the same turbulence, lifted by the site’s sky glow and buried in sensor noise.
simulator.how2: As the stack builds, the turbulence averages out and the image walks toward the aperture’s diffraction limit, which it never beats. This is a simulation of what a 150 mm telescope shows, not a claim about what it captured.

welcome.title: Welcome to the Stellar Observatory
welcome.lead: Ready to connect with the sky? You have four ways to begin:
welcome.text: Drive a telescope live in the console, request a capture from the network, reserve time on Tbilisi One, or browse what the network has photographed. Whether you plan it or pilot it, the sky is yours.
welcome.liveText: Control a telescope in real time — point, adjust settings, and capture frames instantly.
welcome.livePoints: Best for real-time observing|Manual or guided control|Live view and instant capture|Fastest way to explore the sky
welcome.requestsText: Submit a capture request with target, timing and priority. The network schedules, executes and delivers the frame.
welcome.requestsPoints: Built for planned captures|Priority-based scheduling|Routed across the network
welcome.reserveText: Reserve a slot on the network's first instrument for a session of your own.
welcome.reservePoints: Best for planned sessions|A telescope to yourself|Times in your local time
welcome.capturesText: Every frame the network has photographed, with the instrument that took it and where it came from.
welcome.capturesPoints: Browse past captures|Provenance on every frame|Simulated frames labelled as such

guide.title: How to create an astrophoto in 10 minutes
guide.lead: Seven steps from an empty console to a frame of your own.
guide.s1Text: You are here. No account is needed for the simulator — every frame is drawn by the sky model and labelled as such.
guide.s2Text: Open the telescope list and choose a station with a green dot: it is under a dark sky right now. Once connected, the controls appear on the left.
guide.s3Text: Park at zenith, then calibrate. The camera starts during calibration and you should see live stars in the frame.
guide.s4Text: Open the target picker, keep "Visible in your sky" on, and pick something high up. Its coordinates fill in.
guide.s5Text: Point to target and watch the field stream past as the mount slews. Once it is tracking, start the observation — the stack builds and the image sharpens.
guide.s6Text: Capture the current image whenever the view looks right. Each frame is fingerprinted and listed under the view.
guide.s7Text: Simulated frames stay in this session. Real captures from the network are filed under Captures with their provenance.
